title: Contribution to an open-source project
summary: Find an active open-source project, pick a suitable issue, and get a pull request reviewed and merged by following the project's process.
why: A merged pull request is public proof that you can read an unfamiliar codebase, follow a team's conventions and work through code review, which is most of an intern's job. Few student candidates have one.
brief:
Contribute a meaningful change to an established open-source project that you use or find interesting. Meaningful means a bug fix, a small feature, a test covering an untested path, or a substantial documentation improvement, merged by the maintainers. A one-character typo fix is a fine warm-up, but it should not be the headline.

Finding a good first issue: start with tools you already use, such as a Python library, an editor extension or a static site generator. Look for labels like `good first issue`, `help wanted` or `beginner friendly`, and check that the project is alive: recent commits, maintainers who answer issues within a week or two, and pull requests from outside contributors that actually get merged. Read CONTRIBUTING.md and the code of conduct. Choose an issue with a clear description and nobody assigned, comment that you would like to work on it, and wait for a go-ahead if the project asks for one.

Constraints: follow the project's conventions exactly (code style, commit message format, tests, changelog entries). Reproduce the bug or write a failing test before you change anything. Keep the pull request small and focused, explain what and why, and answer review comments promptly and politely. Expect this to take weeks of calendar time, so start early and keep a second issue in mind in case the first one stalls.

milestones.title: Choose a project
tasks: List three projects you use and check each for recent commits, responsive maintainers and merged outside contributions
Read CONTRIBUTING.md and the code of conduct
Join the project's chat or discussion forum if it has one
milestones.doneWhen: You have chosen one active project and can explain in two sentences why it is a good fit.

milestones.title: Build and test locally
tasks: Fork and clone, then follow the setup guide until the test suite runs
Write down any setup problems you hit (fixing the docs can be a first contribution)
Read the code around the area you are interested in
milestones.doneWhen: The project's full test suite passes on your machine.

milestones.title: Claim an issue
tasks: Find an unassigned issue labeled good first issue or help wanted
Reproduce the bug or confirm the missing behavior
Comment with your plan and any questions
milestones.doneWhen: A maintainer has acknowledged your comment (or the guidelines say no claim is needed), and you have reproduced the issue.

milestones.title: Make the change
tasks: Write a failing test that captures the issue
Make the smallest change that fixes it, in the project's style
Run the linters and the full test suite
milestones.doneWhen: Your branch has a test that fails before your change and passes after it, and every existing test still passes.

milestones.title: Pull request and review
tasks: Open a focused pull request that links the issue and explains what changed and why
Answer every review comment and push follow-up commits as asked
milestones.doneWhen: A maintainer has merged your pull request.

milestones.title: Write it up
tasks: Add the merged pull request to your resume and your profile
Write a short post or README section about what you learned
Pick a second issue if you enjoyed the project
milestones.doneWhen: A short write-up exists with the pull request link, the problem, your fix and what review taught you.

stretch: A second merged pull request in the same project
Help triage issues or review another newcomer's pull request
Improve the contributor setup guide based on what confused you
rubric: A reviewer should see a merged pull request in a project with real users and other contributors
A reviewer should see a pull request description that explains the problem, the fix and how it was tested
A reviewer should see a test added or updated alongside the code change
A reviewer should see review comments answered respectfully and completely
A reviewer should see the change follow the project's existing style and conventions
A reviewer should see a short write-up that links the pull request and explains what was learned
showcase: Link the merged pull request directly on your resume, under Projects or an Open Source heading
Write a short post: the issue, how you found your way around the codebase, the review feedback and what you changed
Mention the contribution in your GitHub profile README and in LinkedIn's About or Featured section
resumeBullet: Contributed a merged bug fix to [project] (12k GitHub stars): reproduced a date-parsing error with a failing test, fixed it across 3 modules and worked through two rounds of maintainer review.
interviewTalkingPoints: How you found your way around an unfamiliar codebase (tests, search, a debugger, following call paths)
What the maintainers asked you to change in review, and why they were right
How you chose the issue and checked that the project was active
What you would do differently on your next contribution
